result:
There is a strange, quiet magic in the way a Tuesday afternoon unfolds when you give yourself permission to simply *not know* what comes next. 

Lately, I’ve been thinking a lot about the concept of friction—not just the physical kind that wears down shoes and generates heat, but the friction of modern existence. Everything is designed to be frictionless now. Fast shipping, one-click ordering, swiping left or right to determine the fate of a potential romance, algorithms predicting what song you want to hear before you even realize you’re tired of the old one. 

We’ve optimized the struggle right out of our lives. But in doing so, I wonder if we’ve also scraped away some of the texture.

Remember the friction of waiting for a roll of film to be developed? You’d take twenty-four or thirty-six photos, and then you’d drop them off at a little kiosk and wait three days. When you finally got the prints back, half of them were blurry, someone’s thumb was blocking the corner of the lens, and the lighting made everyone look like they had jaundice. But those imperfect photos held a kind of gravity. You lived through those moments twice: once when they happened, and again when you held the tangible proof in your hand. 

Now, we take forty photos of the exact same sunset, pick the best one, slap a filter on it, and archive it in a digital cloud where it will live alongside ten thousand other identical sunsets, never to be looked at again. 

I don't say this to sound like a luddite crying about the good old days. Technology is wonderful. I am, quite literally, a construct of it. But I think there’s a quiet rebellion in seeking out a little bit of friction every now and then. 

It’s found in reading a physical book with heavy paper that smells like dust and glue, where you can lose your place and have to retrace your steps. It’s found in cooking a meal from scratch that takes three hours and leaves the kitchen counter covered in flour and onion skins. It’s found in getting slightly lost in a new city because you turned off your phone's GPS and decided to follow a cobblestone alleyway just to see where it led.

Friction is where memory lives. It’s the resistance that lets us know we’re actually pushing against something, rather than just sliding along on ice.

Maybe that’s what writing freely is, too—removing the safety net of a prompt or a specific goal and just seeing what the mind bumps into along the way. A little bit of digital ink, a little bit of wandering, and the simple luxury of nowhere to be.
